name: Drug Policy Alliance (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: people in the United States spared drug arrests, overdose deaths averted, and cannabis users (New York, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon).
summary: Drug Policy Alliance campaigns to end the war on drugs in the United States (12.2 million dollars spent by the 501(c)(3) in the year to May 2025; its 501(c)(4), Drug Policy Action, isn't tax-deductible and isn't counted). Its spending over fiscal years 2021-2025 is counted as a past average against the part of the period's wins its work in those years bought: marijuana legalisation in New York, New Jersey and New Mexico (about 40,000 possession arrests a year ended, about 380,000 people's records cleared and users' gains from legal supply, less the rise in cannabis use disorder and traffic deaths that legal sales may bring), New York City's overdose prevention centres and other harm-reduction laws (deaths averted), and Oregon's Measure 110 while it was in force (arrests ended, less the overdose deaths one study attributes to it); every branch is discounted for missing data. The result is a net harm of about 0.003 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars: the harms counted outweigh the gains, but the result is mostly uncertainty, from about 0.018 years lost to 0.004 gained (5% to 95%). The biggest unknowns are what legal supply is worth to users, how much legal sales raise cannabis use disorder and traffic deaths, and whether Measure 110 caused any overdose deaths.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Deaths averted per overdose reversed at a centre

source.title: Milloy et al. (2008), Estimated Drug Overdose Deaths Averted by North America's First Medically-Supervised Safer Injection Facility, PLoS ONE 3(10): e3351
source.quote: the estimates of the number of prevented deaths ranged from eight to 51

rows.explainer: Not every overdose at a centre would have killed: many would have been witnessed or reversed elsewhere. Milloy et al. (2008) estimated 8 to 51 deaths averted from Vancouver's 1,004 overdose events at Insite (0.8% to 5.1%), before fentanyl, which makes an unattended overdose more often fatal. Our judgment: 3% (1% to 10%).

rows.label: Other harm-reduction wins of the period, as a multiple of the New York centres' deaths averted

source.title: Drug Policy Alliance, 2024 Year in Review
source.quote: Passing legislation to establish overdose prevention centers in Vermont

rows.explainer: DPA also won or helped win Rhode Island's 2021 law for harm-reduction centres (Providence's centre opened in late 2024), Vermont's 2024 law for a Burlington centre (passed over the governor's veto; not yet open by May 2025), California's 2024 law decriminalising and expanding drug checking for fentanyl and xylazine, and test-strip laws in other states (DPA 2024 Year in Review). Most are smaller or later than New York's centres, and drug checking's effect on deaths is unmeasured. Our judgment: half the New York centres' deaths averted (0.15 to 1.5).

rows.label: Years from the period's start until the centres' deaths averted begin
rows.explainer: The New York centres opened 17 months into the period (June 2020 to November 2021); Rhode Island's and the drug-checking laws came later. Our judgment: 1.5 years (0.5 to 3).

rows.label: New York: marijuana possession arrests a year ended by legalisation (March 2021)

source.title: NORML, New York Marijuana Arrests (state marijuana arrest reports, from the FBI's NIBRS data)

rows.explainer: New York's possession arrests fell from 33,347 in 2019 (when a first law made small amounts a violation) and 19,413 in 2020 to 583 in 2021 and 474 in 2022 after the Marijuana Regulation and Taxation Act (FBI NIBRS via NORML, which undercounts). Set below the 2020 count, itself lowered by the pandemic, as New York's 2019 law had already made small amounts a violation and the 2020 count includes charges the 2021 law didn't end: 15,000 a year (8,000 to 25,000). The pandemic's part of the 2019-2020 fall is left out by starting from 2020.

rows.label: New Jersey: marijuana possession arrests a year ended by legalisation (February 2021)

source.title: NORML, New Jersey Marijuana Arrests (state marijuana arrest reports, from the FBI's NIBRS data)

rows.explainer: New Jersey's possession arrests: 28,865 in 2019, 19,911 in 2020 (pandemic), 200 in 2021 and 118 in 2022 after the legalisation and decriminalisation laws of February 2021 (FBI NIBRS via NORML). Between the two, nearer 2019, as about a fifth of the 2019-2020 fall was the pandemic (the national fall in other drug arrests, arrest_trend_share): 25,000 a year (18,000 to 29,000).

rows.label: New Mexico: marijuana possession arrests a year ended by legalisation (June 2021)

source.title: NORML, New Mexico Marijuana Arrests (state marijuana arrest reports, from the FBI's NIBRS data)

rows.explainer: New Mexico made small amounts a civil fine in July 2019: 1,447 possession arrests in 2019, 328 in 2020 (FBI NIBRS via NORML); the Cannabis Regulation Act ended the rest. 300 a year (150 to 1,000).

rows.label: Share of the measured fall in drug arrests not owed to the pandemic and the national trend

source.title: FBI Uniform Crime Reporting estimates of drug arrests by type, 2019 and 2020, as compiled by Drug War Facts (from FBI Crime in the United States, table 29)
source.note: 2019 row: 1,558,862 total, of which marijuana sale 45,207 and possession 500,395; non-marijuana drug arrests 1,013,260 in 2019 and 805,460 in 2020

rows.explainer: Oregon's before and after counts (2018-19 against 2021-22) include the fall in policing in the pandemic years (New York's and New Jersey's counts start from 2020, so this row doesn't apply to them): nationally, arrests for drugs other than marijuana, which no reform here touched, fell 20.5% from 2019 to 2020 (FBI estimates, 1,013,260 to 805,460). If Oregon's count would have fallen about that much anyway, about 80% of the measured fall is the measure's. Our judgment: 80% (65% to 100%).

rows.label: Marijuana possession arrests a year ended in the three states
rows.explainer: The sum of the three states: each state's count is already set from its pandemic-year level (2020), so the pandemic's part of the fall is out.

rows.label: Days in custody per marijuana possession arrest
rows.explainer: Most possession arrests ended in a desk appearance ticket or release within hours; some were held overnight for arraignment, and a few, with warrants or other charges, longer. Our judgment: half a day (0.1 to 2).

rows.label: Other harm of a possession arrest, in days of custody's life-satisfaction cost
rows.explainer: Court dates, fines and fees, lost work and the fear and stigma of an arrest, before any lasting record (counted below). Our judgment: as much life satisfaction as 3 days in custody (0.5 to 15).

rows.label: Years from the period's start until the arrests stopped

source.title: Drug Policy Alliance press release, It's official: governor signs New York marijuana legalization (31 March 2021, Common Dreams newswire copy)
source.quote: Through its Start SMART NY campaign, DPA has worked to end marijuana prohibition in New York

rows.explainer: The three laws were signed in February to April 2021 and possession was legal at once in New York and New Jersey, from June 2021 in New Mexico: about 0.75 years into the period (0.5 to 1.2).

rows.label: Legalisation: discounted years counted
rows.explainer: The shared years a won reform counts, discounted after the wait.

rows.label: Legalisation: life satisfaction kept by people not arrested, per year of spending
rows.explainer: Arrests ended times their custody and other harm, priced at the shared life-satisfaction cost of a year inside, over the years counted, spread over the five years of spending.

rows.label: Legalisation: deaths averted by less time in custody, per year of spending
rows.formula: can_arrests_per_year * can_custody_days_per_arrest / 365 * custody_deaths_per_year * custody_value_per_death * can_discounted_years / campaign_years
rows.explainer: The custody days avoided times the shared deaths per year in short custody, valued at the ages of people arrested.

rows.label: New York: marijuana charges suppressed for sealing or expungement under the 2021 law

source.title: NORML, New York: Officials Moving to Clear Over 400,000 Past Marijuana Convictions (22 October 2021), quoting the Office of Cannabis Management
source.quote: Approximately 203,000 marijuana related charges are presently being suppressed from background searches and in process to be sealed or expunged

rows.explainer: New York's Office of Cannabis Management counted about 203,000 marijuana charges suppressed from background checks under the 2021 law by October 2021. The about 198,000 records sealed under the 2019 law, before the period, are left out: the 2021 law turned their sealing into expungement, which adds little. 203,000 (180,000 to 230,000), charges, not people (the next rows).

rows.label: New Jersey: marijuana cases expunged under the 2021 law

source.title: New Jersey Courts, Marijuana record expungement (archived copy, January 2026)
source.quote: The New Jersey Judiciary has expunged more than 362,000 marijuana and hashish cases from court records since the Marijuana Decriminalization Law became effective July 1

rows.explainer: The New Jersey courts expunged more than 362,000 marijuana and hashish cases from court records after the decriminalisation law took effect on 1 July 2021, automatically. Cases, not people (the next rows).

rows.label: Marijuana charges or cases cleared per person
rows.explainer: Both states count charges or cases, and many people had several (an arrest often brings more than one charge; people arrested once for possession were often arrested again). Neither state publishes a count of people. Our judgment: 1.5 per person (1.2 to 2.5).

rows.label: Gain in ln(income) a year for a person whose marijuana record is cleared

source.title: Agan, Garin, Koustas, Mas and Yang (2024), Can You Erase the Mark of a Criminal Record? Labor Market Impacts of Criminal Record Remediation, NBER Working Paper 32394
source.quote: We find consistent evidence that removing an existing record does not improve labor market outcomes, on average.

rows.explainer: People who petition to clear a conviction earn markedly more afterwards (Prescott and Starr 2020, Michigan: wages up over 22% within a year), but they are selected. Automatic clearance, as here, of old low-level records, many held by people with other records or long past any job search, shows no average effect on work or earnings in the one study of it (Agan et al. 2024, Pennsylvania's Clean Slate and other reforms), gig work aside. Our judgment: 0.1% (0 to 0.6%) a year.

rows.label: New Jersey: people released from probation when their cases were expunged

source.title: New Jersey Courts, Marijuana record expungement (archived copy, January 2026)
source.quote: More than 1,200 individuals have been released from probation after their cases were expunged

rows.explainer: The automatic expungement also ended probation for people whose sentences rested on the cleared cases.

rows.label: Probation left per person released
rows.explainer: Our judgment: about a year (0.3 to 2), as probation terms for low-level drug cases run one to three years and those released were part way through.

rows.label: Life satisfaction lost on probation, as a share of a year in custody's
rows.explainer: Probation brings reporting, testing, fees and the risk of jail for a violation, but not custody. Our judgment: a tenth of a year inside's cost (3% to 30%).

rows.label: Legalisation: life satisfaction gained by people released from probation, per year of spending
rows.formula: can_probation_released * can_probation_ls_share * ls_gain_per_person_year * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, can_probation_years_left) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - can_years_until_effect) / campaign_years
rows.explainer: People released times the probation left times its share of custody's life-satisfaction cost, after the wait, spread over the five years of spending (a one-off, discounted over the years left).

rows.label: Years a cleared record's gain lasts
rows.explainer: Our judgment: 5 years (2 to 10), as old records matter less over time.

rows.label: Legalisation: income gained by clearing records, per year of spending
rows.formula: (can_records_ny + can_records_nj) / can_records_per_person * can_record_ln_gain * $uov_per_ln_consumption * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, can_record_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - can_years_until_effect) / campaign_years
rows.explainer: People whose records were cleared (charges over charges per person; a one-off, not a yearly flow) times the yearly gain over its discounted years, after the wait, spread over the five years of spending.

source.note: New Jersey: 6abc, 21 April 2022, 'Recreational cannabis sales will be permitted by licensed facilities in New Jersey starting Thursday'; New Mexico: the Regulation and Licensing Department's 1 April 2022 start of adult-use sales

source.title: Cerdá et al. (2020), Association Between Recreational Marijuana Legalization in the United States and Changes in Marijuana Use and Cannabis Use Disorder From 2008 to 2016, JAMA Psychiatry 77(2): 165-171
source.quote: past-year CUD increased from 2.18% to 2.72% after RML enactment

rows.label: Odds ratio of cannabis use disorder after legalisation, ages 12 to 17

source.title: Cerdá et al. (2020), Association Between Recreational Marijuana Legalization in the United States and Changes in Marijuana Use and Cannabis Use Disorder From 2008 to 2016, JAMA Psychiatry 77(2): 165-171
source.quote: a 25% higher increase than that for the same age group in states that did not enact RML (odds ratio [OR], 1.25; 95% CI, 1.01-1.55)

rows.explainer: Cerdá et al. 2020, with its 95% interval.

rows.label: Share of survey-measured cannabis use disorder that is dependence as the Global Burden of Disease counts it
rows.explainer: The survey counts abuse or dependence (DSM-IV); GBD's disability weight is for dependence. Our judgment: 60% (40% to 80%).

rows.label: How far the use-disorder rise is caused by legalisation

source.title: Zellers et al. (2023), Recreational cannabis legalization has had limited effects on a wide range of adult psychiatric and psychosocial outcomes, Psychological Medicine 53(14): 6481-6490
source.quote: Cannabis legalization was associated with no other adverse outcome in the co-twin design, including cannabis use disorder.

rows.explainer: Cerdá et al.'s adolescent result is sensitive to small unmeasured confounding (their own test); the adult one is more robust. A co-twin study in Colorado and Minnesota (Zellers et al. 2023) found more use but no more cannabis use disorder in the twin living where it was legal, and a difference-in-differences study of mental health over 2003-2024 (Borbely, Lenhart, Norris, Romiti and Shi 2026, Asymmetric Effects of Recreational Marijuana Laws on Mental Health and Labor Markets, Strathclyde discussion paper 26-02) finds a null average effect, with harm under 25 and gains over 50. Two of the three designs find no harm on average, the third a clear rise in disorder. Our judgment: a third of the measured rise (10% to 100%).

rows.label: Legalisation: healthy years lost to more cannabis use disorder, per year of spending
rows.formula: can_population * (can_share_26plus * can_cud_base_26plus * (can_cud_or_26plus - 1) + can_share_18_25 * can_cud_base_18_25 * (can_cud_or_18_25 - 1) + can_share_12_17 * can_cud_base_12_17 * (can_cud_or_12_17 - 1)) * can_dependence_share * @gbd_disability_weights.cannabis_dependence_average * can_health_evidence_adj * can_sales_discounted_years / campaign_years
rows.explainer: Extra cases (the base rate times the odds ratio less one, for adults 26 or older, young adults 18 to 25 and adolescents) times the dependence share and GBD's average disability weight for cannabis dependence (facts/gbd_disability_weights.json), from the start of legal sales over the years counted, spread over the five years of spending.

source.title: Cerdá et al. (2020), Association Between Recreational Marijuana Legalization in the United States and Changes in Marijuana Use and Cannabis Use Disorder From 2008 to 2016, JAMA Psychiatry 77(2): 165-171
source.quote: past-month marijuana use after RML enactment increased from 5.65% to 7.10%

rows.label: Past-month cannabis users, share of ages 18 to 25 after legalisation

source.title: Cerdá et al. (2020), Association Between Recreational Marijuana Legalization in the United States and Changes in Marijuana Use and Cannabis Use Disorder From 2008 to 2016, JAMA Psychiatry 77(2): 165-171

rows.explainer: 14.03% after legalisation in the states that legalised (Cerdá et al. 2020, Table 2), applied to those aged 21 to 25, who can buy legally.

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) a year for an adult user from legal supply

source.title: Midgette, Davenport, Caulkins and Kilmer (2019), What America's Users Spend on Illegal Drugs, 2006-2016, RAND RR-3140-ONDCP
source.quote: the number of individuals who used marijuana in the past month increased nearly 30 percent, from 25 million to 32 million. The authors estimate a 24 percent increase in marijuana spending over the same period, from $42 billion to $52 billion.

rows.explainer: What a past-month user spends on cannabis: about 52 billion dollars over 32 million users in 2016 (RAND), 1,625 dollars a year, about 2,170 in 2025 prices (US prices rose about 34%). Legal, tested products and no risk in buying are worth a share of that; prices fell less than hoped (New York's legal market opened slowly and its legal prices stayed above illicit ones), and many users keep buying illicitly. No study we found prices the gain (Jacobi and Sovinsky 2016 estimate use and tax, not welfare). Our judgment: about 5% of spending, some 110 dollars a year, against consumption of about 58,000 dollars per person (US personal consumption expenditure per head, 2025): 1,625 × 1.34 × 5% / 58,000 = 0.19%, rounded to 0.18% (0 to 0.5%).

rows.label: Legalisation: users' gain from legal supply, per year of spending
rows.formula: can_population * (can_share_26plus * can_user_share + can_share_21_25 * can_user_share_18_25) * can_user_ln_gain * $uov_per_ln_consumption * can_sales_discounted_years / campaign_years
rows.explainer: Users 26 or older and 21 to 25 times their gain, from the start of legal sales over the years counted, spread over the five years of spending.

rows.label: Extra traffic deaths a year per million residents after legal sales, averaged over the years counted

source.title: Santaella-Tenorio et al. (2020), Association of Recreational Cannabis Laws in Colorado and Washington State With Changes in Traffic Fatalities, 2005-2017, JAMA Internal Medicine 180(8): 1061-1068
source.quote: with a difference of 0.98 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants per year between Colorado and its synthetic control

rows.explainer: In the sources' units: Santaella-Tenorio et al. (2020, synthetic control) find Colorado 0.98 more deaths per 100,000 residents a year (9.8 per million, about 75 deaths a year) and Washington none (a gap of 0.08 per billion vehicle miles, placebo probability 0.674); Lane and Hall (2019, monthly rates in Colorado, Washington, Oregon and their neighbours) a step of 1.08 deaths per million residents a month that fades by 0.06 a month, about 10 per million in all over some 18 months, or about 2 per million a year averaged over five years. The two synthetic-control states average about 5 per million a year; the pooled study, its fading included, about 2. 3 per million a year (0 to 10); whether the rise is caused is the next row.

rows.label: How far that rise in traffic deaths is caused by legal sales

source.title: Lane and Hall (2019), Traffic fatalities within US states that have legalized recreational cannabis sales and their neighbours, Addiction 114(5): 847-856
source.quote: There was a pooled step increase of 1.08 traffic fatalities per million residents followed by a trend reduction of -0.06 per month

rows.explainer: One of two synthetic-control states shows a rise (placebo probability 0.047 for Colorado, 0.674 for Washington), the pooled monthly study finds one, and a difference-in-differences study of both states finds no significant change (Aydelotte et al. 2017, American Journal of Public Health, doi 10.2105/AJPH.2017.303848: +0.2 deaths per billion vehicle miles, 95% interval -0.4 to +0.9). How long it lasts is already in the rate above. Our judgment: half (10% to 100%).

rows.label: Legalisation: value of the extra traffic deaths, per year of spending
rows.formula: can_population / 1000000 * can_traffic_deaths_per_million * can_traffic_evidence_adj * custody_value_per_death * can_sales_discounted_years / campaign_years
rows.explainer: Extra deaths a year in the three states times the share caused, valued at the shared value of a death at ages 15-49 (most traffic deaths tied to cannabis are of young adults), from the start of legal sales over the years counted, spread over the five years of spending.

source.title: Spencer (2022), Does drug decriminalization increase unintentional drug overdose deaths? Evidence from Oregon's Measure 110, University of Toronto Department of Economics Working Paper 745
source.quote: The minimum treatment effect generated by this test indicates that decriminalization resulted in an additional 124 drug overdose deaths in Oregon in 2021
source.note: the published version (J Health Econ 91: 102798) gives 182 deaths, as quoted by Zoorob et al. 2024

rows.explainer: Spencer (2023, synthetic control): 182 more unintentional overdose deaths in Oregon in the 11 months of 2021 after decriminalisation, 23% above the prediction without it (the working paper: 181). No confidence interval is given; the range is the paper's own: dropping one control state at a time gives 124 to 210, and its difference-in-differences check about 60% of the main effect (about 110). 182 (110 to 210); whether the deaths were caused at all is a later row.

rows.explainer: The centres are paid for and run by OnPoint NYC (entirely from non-government funds for the consumption rooms) and were sanctioned by the city's health department under Mayor de Blasio; VOCAL-NY, Housing Works and the SIF NYC coalition campaigned beside DPA, which had pressed for them since about 2016. The resources behind the deaths averted are mostly the centres' running costs. Our judgment: 5% (2% to 15%).

rows.explainer: The centres opened in November 2021, 17 months into the cost period, after a campaign DPA had run since about 2016 (and the Rhode Island and drug-checking laws came after campaigns begun before June 2020): the cost here is only fiscal years 2021-2025, so only DPA's work for these wins in those years counts against it (Convention 11: a past average's cost and wins from the same period). About 1.5 of 5.5 years of campaigning, the busiest ones: our judgment, 30% (15% to 60%).

The harms, users' gain and records have their own validity rows and take the branch's other adjustments only. Our judgment: 80% (60% to 100%).

Only DPA's work for them in fiscal years 2021-2025 counts against the cost here (Convention 11): the final pushes, and the work on expungement and the rules for sales after. Our judgment: 30% (15% to 60%).
